The figure shows a square with four circles of equal area, each touching two sides of the square and two other circles. What is the ratio between the area of the black region and the total area of the grey regions?

solutions.title: Split the square into four quarters
solutions.body:
Each circle is inscribed in one of four equal quarter-squares. In each quarter, the part outside the circle consists of four equal 'corner' pieces. One of these corners (the one at the centre of the big square) is black and the other three are grey. So in each quarter, and therefore in the whole figure, the black and grey areas are in the ratio $1:3$.

**Answer: (B) 1 : 3**

prompt: 232 and 111 are both three-digit palindromes as they read the same from left to right as they do right to left. What is the sum of the digits of the largest three-digit palindrome that is also a multiple of 6?
Tom draws a square. He adds a regular hexagon, one side of which joins the centre of the square to one of the vertices of the square, as shown. What is the size of angle $\alpha$?

Sadinie is asked to create a rectangular enclosure using 40 m of fencing so that the side-lengths, in metres, of the enclosure are all prime numbers. What is the maximum possible area of the enclosure?

solutions.title: List prime pairs with sum 20
solutions.body:
The length and width add up to $40\div2=20$ m. Pairs of primes with sum 20 are $3+17$ and $7+13$ (an even sum of two primes needs two odd primes; $1$ is not prime). The areas are $3\times17=51$ and $7\times13=91$. The maximum is $91\ \text{m}^2$.

**Answer: (C) $91\ \text{m}^2$**

prompt: Lil writes one of the letters P, Q, R, S in each cell of a $2\times4$ table. She does this in such a way that, in each row and in each $2\times2$ square, all four letters appear. In how many ways can she do this?

The diagram gives the lengths of six lines meeting at a point. Eric wishes to redraw this diagram without lifting his pencil from the paper. He can choose to start his drawing anywhere. What is the shortest distance he can draw to reproduce the figure?

solutions.title: Start and end on the longest lines
solutions.body:
The six lines have lengths 3, 2, 2, 1, 1, 1, total 10 cm. To redraw without lifting the pencil, each line must be drawn out from the centre, and then every line except the first and last must be drawn back again. The pencil starts at the end of one line and finishes at the end of another, so those two lines are drawn once and the other four lines are drawn twice.

To minimise the distance, start and finish on the two longest lines (3 cm and 2 cm): total $3+2+2\times(2+1+1+1)=5+10=15$ cm.

**Answer: (B) 15 cm**

prompt: A rectangle is divided into three regions of equal area. One of the regions is an equilateral triangle with side-length 4 cm; and the other two are trapezia, as shown. What is the length of the smaller of the parallel sides of the trapezia?
The ages of Jo, her daughter and her grandson are all even numbers. The product of their three ages is 2024. How old is Jo?

solutions.title: Factorise 2024
solutions.body:
Write the ages as $2j$, $2d$, $2g$. Then $8jdg=2024$, so $jdg=253=11\times23$. Since 1 is also allowed, the ages are $2\times1=2$, $2\times11=22$ and $2\times23=46$. Jo is the oldest, so she is 46.

**Answer: (C) 46**

prompt: The sum of the digits of the positive integer $N$ is three times the sum of the digits of $N+1$. What is the smallest possible sum of the digits of $N$?

solutions.title: The digit sum falls only when N ends in 9
solutions.body:
Adding 1 raises the digit sum by 1 unless $N$ ends in 9. If $N$ ends in exactly one 9, then adding 1 turns the 9 into 0 and adds 1 to the tens digit, so the digit sum falls by 8. Let the digit sum of $N$ be $x$; then $x=3(x-8)$, so $x=12$. For example $N=39$: digit sum $12$, and $N+1=40$ has digit sum $4$.

If $N$ ends in two or more 9s, its digit sum is at least $19$, which is larger. So the smallest is 12.

**Answer: (B) 12**

prompt: Polly has three circles cut from three pieces of coloured card. She originally places them on top of each other as shown. In this configuration the area of the visible black region is seven times the area of the white circle. Polly moves the circles to a new position, as shown, with each pair of circles touching each other. What is the ratio between the areas of the visible black regions before and after?

A point is chosen inside an equilateral triangle. From this point we draw three segments parallel to the sides, as shown. The lengths of the segments are 2 m, 3 m and 6 m. What is the perimeter of the triangle?

solutions.title: Extend the segments
solutions.body:
Extend the three segments to the sides of the triangle. The base then consists of two parallelograms and a small equilateral triangle: along the base we find the lengths 2 m, 3 m and 6 m (each equal to the opposite side of a parallelogram, or a side of a small equilateral triangle). So the side of the big triangle is $2+3+6=11$ m, and its perimeter is $3\times11=33$ m.

**Answer: (C) 33 m**

The sides, in cm, of two squares are integers. The difference between the areas of the two squares is $19\ \text{cm}^2$. What is the sum of the perimeters of the two squares?

solutions.title: Difference of squares
solutions.body:
Let the sides be $x>y$. Then $x^2-y^2=(x+y)(x-y)=19$. Since 19 is prime and $x+y>x-y$, we get $x+y=19$ and $x-y=1$. The sum of the perimeters is $4x+4y=4\times19=76$ cm.

**Answer: (E) 76 cm**

solutions.title: Find the sides
solutions.body:
From $x+y=19$ and $x-y=1$: $x=10$, $y=9$. Check: $100-81=19$ ✓. Perimeters $40+36=76$ cm.

**Answer: (E) 76 cm**

prompt: Matthew rolled a normal die 24 times. All numbers from 1 to 6 came up at least once. The number 1 came up more times than any other number. Matthew added up all the numbers. The total he obtained was the largest one possible. What total did he obtain?

For some positive integer $n$, the prime factorisation of the number $n!=1\times2\times\dots\times n$ is of the form shown in the figure; the primes are written in increasing order. Ink has covered some of the primes and some of the exponents. What is the exponent of 17?

solutions.title: Find n
solutions.body:
The largest prime visible is 47, and the next prime 53 does not appear, so $47\le n<53$. The prime 13 has exponent 4, so there are exactly four multiples of 13 up to $n$: 13, 26, 39, 52. Thus $n\ge52$ and $n<65$, so $n=52$.

The multiples of 17 up to 52 are 17, 34 and 51, so the exponent of 17 is 3.

**Answer: (C) 3**

prompt: Kevin makes a net using a combination of squares and equilateral triangles, as shown in the figure. The side length of each square and of each triangle is 1 cm. He folds the net up to form the surface of a polyhedron. What is the distance between the vertices $J$ and $K$ in this polyhedron?

solutions.title: Identify the solid
solutions.body:
The four squares fold into a square tube (the side faces of a cube of side 1). The four triangles at the top fold into a square-based pyramid with apex $K$ closing the top, and the four at the bottom form a similar pyramid with apex $J$. So the distance $JK$ is the height of the cube plus the heights of the two pyramids.

Each pyramid has a base square of side 1 and slant edges 1. The half-diagonal of the base is $\tfrac{\sqrt2}{2}$, so the height of the pyramid is $\sqrt{1-\tfrac12}=\tfrac{\sqrt2}{2}$. Therefore $JK=\tfrac{\sqrt2}{2}+1+\tfrac{\sqrt2}{2}=1+\sqrt2$ cm.

**Answer: (B) $(1+\sqrt2)$ cm**

prompt: Jill has some unit cubes which are all black, grey, or white. She uses 27 of them to build a $3\times3\times3$ cube. She wants the surface to be exactly one-third black, one-third grey, and one-third white. The smallest possible number of black cubes she can use is $X$ and the largest possible number of black cubes she can use is $Y$. What is the value of $Y-X$?

solutions.title: Count visible faces
solutions.body:
The surface has $6\times9=54$ unit faces, so 18 must be black. A corner cube shows 3 faces, an edge cube 2, a face-centre cube 1, and the cube at the very centre shows none. There are 8 corners, 12 edges and 6 face-centres.

To use as few black cubes as possible use the cubes showing most faces: 6 corner cubes show $6\times3=18$ faces, so $X=6$.

To use as many as possible, use the cubes showing fewest faces: the 6 face-centres (6 faces) and 6 edge cubes (12 faces) give $6+12=18$ faces with 12 cubes, and the hidden central cube can also be black. So $Y=13$.

$Y-X=13-6=7$.

**Answer: (D) 7**

prompt: Meera walked in the park. She walked half of the total time at a speed of 2 km/h. She then walked half of the total distance at a speed of 3 km/h. Finally, she completed the remainder of the walk at a speed of 4 km/h. For what fraction of the total time did she walk at a speed of 4 km/h?

Given the integers from 1 to 25, Ajibola wants to remove a few and then split those that remain into two groups so that the products of the integers in each group are equal. Ajibola removes the smallest possible number of integers in order to achieve this. What is the sum of the numbers which Ajibola removes?

solutions.title: Prime factors must pair up
solutions.body:
If the two groups have equal products, every prime must occur to an even power in the product of all remaining numbers. The primes 13, 17, 19, 23 each divide only one number up to 25 (13, 17, 19, 23 themselves; $2\times13=26>25$), so these four numbers must be removed.

For 7 the multiples are 7, 14, 21: exponent 3, which is odd, so at least one multiple of 7 must go; removing 7 itself fixes this without changing any other prime. The exponents of 2, 3, 5, 11 in $25!$ are $22$, $10$, $6$, $2$, all even, so no more removals are needed. So at least 5 numbers are removed: $7,13,17,19,23$, with sum $79$.

They do work: for example $3\times5\times8\times14\times15\times18\times20\times22\times24=2\times4\times6\times9\times10\times11\times12\times16\times21\times25=2^{11}3^55^37\cdot11$.

**Answer: (B) 79**

prompt: Twenty points are equally spaced around the circumference of a circle. Kevin draws all the possible chords that connect pairs of these points. How many of these chords are longer than the radius of the circle but shorter than its diameter?

There are $n$ distinct lines in the plane. One of these lines intersects exactly 5 of the $n$ lines, another of these intersects exactly 9 of the $n$ lines, and yet another intersects exactly 11 of them. Which of the following is the smallest possible value of $n$?

solutions.title: Lower bound and construction
solutions.body:
One line meets 11 others, so $n\ge12$. For $n=12$: take 7 parallel lines, 3 parallel lines in another direction, and 2 further lines not parallel to anything else. A line of the first family meets the 3 lines of the second family and the 2 extra lines: $5$ lines. A line of the second family meets the 7 lines of the first family and the 2 extra lines: $9$ lines. Each extra line meets all other 11 lines.

So $n=12$ works.

**Answer: (A) 12**

prompt: Suppose $m$ and $n$ are integers with $0<m<n$. Let $P=(m,n)$, $Q=(n,m)$ and $O=(0,0)$. For how many pairs of $m$ and $n$ will the area of triangle $OPQ$ be equal to 2024?

solutions.title: Area as a difference of squares
solutions.body:
The points $P$ and $Q$ are symmetric about the line $y=x$. Taking $PQ$ as base, $PQ=\sqrt2\,(n-m)$, and the midpoint of $PQ$ is $\left(\tfrac{n+m}2,\tfrac{n+m}2\right)$, whose distance from $O$ is $\tfrac{n+m}{\sqrt2}$. The area is $\tfrac12\sqrt2(n-m)\cdot\tfrac{n+m}{\sqrt2}=\tfrac{(n+m)(n-m)}2$.

So $(n+m)(n-m)=4048=2^4\times11\times23$. The factors $n+m$ and $n-m$ have the same parity, so both are even, and $n+m>n-m$. Write $n+m=2a$, $n-m=2b$ with $ab=1012=2^2\times11\times23$, $a>b$, and $b\ge1$; also $m=a-b>0$. The number of divisors of 1012 is $3\times2\times2=12$, giving 6 pairs with $a>b$. So there are 6 pairs $(m,n)$.

**Answer: (B) 6**
